# What Are the California WARN Act 2026 Changes?

On Behalf Of Elite Trial Group| May 19, 2026 | FAQs

The California WARN Act 2026 changes expand what employers must put in writing when they lay off workers, close a worksite, or relocate operations. The new law, Senate Bill 617, took effect January 1, 2026 and amends California Labor Code Section 1401. It does not change the 60-day notice requirement. It changes what the notice must say.

Most workers getting handed a WARN notice in 2026 have no idea the rules shifted. They see the 60-day notice, sign for it, and start planning their last day. What they do not realize is that California now requires employers to include specific information about job placement services, food assistance benefits, and workforce development contacts. A notice that leaves any of this out is defective, and a defective notice can be the foundation of a WARN Act claim worth up to 60 days of back pay and benefits per affected worker.

This post breaks down what the California WARN Act 2026 changes require, what rights they create for workers, what employers are still getting wrong, and what to do if you received a notice that does not comply.

1. Severance and the pay-in-lieu calculus
2. What to watch

On April 14, Oakland City University, a small private institution in Gibson County, Indiana, sent a WARN notice to the state and to at least some of its employees, stating it was "currently anticipating the need to implement a mass layoff." Within weeks, university officials were telling reporters the school did not actually plan to conduct layoffs. Instead, they said, OCU was hoping to sell a carbon-capture patent to shore up its finances. Then, in May, the paychecks stopped arriving altogether, twice.

The sequence is worth studying not because it is unusual but because it is unusually transparent. Most companies that file a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification do not walk it back publicly. They file, wait the mandatory 60 days, and cut. But OCU's filing, reported by the Evansville Courier & Press, inadvertently revealed what the WARN Act actually produces in 2026: not a cushion for workers, but a distress signal that travels faster than the official story. The notice became a public ledger entry before the university had a rescue narrative ready.

## On April 14, 2026, Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen signed into a new state-level Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act, which requires employers with one hundred or more employees to provide a ninety-day advance notice of mass layoffs and covered business closings.

Listen to “Nebraska Enacts State WARN Law”

Quick Hits

- A new law in Nebraska (Legislative Bill 921) requires employers with one hundred or more workers to provide notice at least ninety days before a mass layoff or business closing.
- The law stipulates certain information that must be included in the layoff notices and how the notices may be delivered.
- The law will take effect on July 18, 2026.

Nebraska’s mini-WARN Act, enacted under Legislative Bill (LB) 921, defines “mass layoff” as a “reduction in employment force that is not the result of a business closing and results in an employment loss at a single site of employment during any thirty-day period of one hundred or more employees,” not including part-time employees.

A business closing means “the permanent or temporary shutdown of a single site of employment of one or more facilities or operating units that will result in an employment loss for one hundred or more employees, other than part-time employees.”

1. The Classification Loophole

On March 31, 2026, Oracle sent termination notices by email to an estimated 20,000 to 30,000 employees, the largest single layoff event in the company's history, Forbes reported. The same quarter, Oracle posted $553 million in net income. The severance offer came with a condition that caught the attention of employment lawyers and labor economists alike: sign a release of claims first, and only then receive the payout. No negotiation. No counteroffer. The company had structured the separations so that many workers did not qualify for the 60-day advance notice required under the federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act, according to TechCrunch, because Oracle classified them under exemptions built into the 1988 law.

The WARN Act requires employers with 100 or more full-time workers to provide 60 calendar days' notice before a plant closing or a mass layoff affecting 50 or more employees at a single site. The statute, passed in an era when a layoff meant a factory gate closing and not a Slack channel going dark, was designed to give workers and their communities time to prepare. # Diamond Transportation Services (Maryland) WARN Act Investigation

Strauss Borrelli PLLC, a leading class action law firm, is investigating Diamond Transportation Services Inc., a National Express / WeDriveU company regarding its recent potential mass layoff in Landover, Maryland. The WARN Act is a federal law that requires certain employers to notify their employees, in writing, at least 60 days before a plant closing or mass layoff takes effect. As a result, we believe Diamond Transportation Services employees may be entitled to 60 days of severance pay and benefits.

WHAT HAPPENED?

On May 12, 2026, Diamond Transportation Services notified the Maryland Department of Labor of its decision to conduct a mass layoff at its facility in Landover, Maryland. The federal law, known as the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act, requires covered employers to provide 60 days’ prior written notice to employees, their representatives, and certain government parties in the event of a mass layoff or plant closing. We are investigating whether Diamond Transportation Services failed to provide at least 60 days’ notice before laying off 571 employees and, therefore, violated the WARN Act.

results.title: Oracle's March 31 Layoff: 25,000 Engineers, 491 WARN Filings, Zero Badges · Refolk
results.text:
Oracle's March 31 Layoff: 25,000 Engineers, 491 WARN Filings, Zero Badges · Refolk

On March 31, 2026, Oracle sent 6 a.m. termination emails to somewhere between 20,000 and 30,000 employees and said nothing publicly. Two months later, WARN filings cover 491 people in Washington state, the Open to Work badge count is a rounding error against the real headcount, and Meta's May 20 wave is about to bury whatever public signal remains. If you source technical talent, this is the largest invisible cohort on the market right now.

## The paper trail that isn't there

Oracle's March cuts are unusual not because of the size (TD Cowen pegs them at 18% of a 162,000-person workforce) but because of how thoroughly they evaded the normal sourcing trail. The company never confirmed a number. It did not address the cuts on its Q3 FY2026 earnings call. It disclosed a $2.1 billion restructuring charge in the 10-Q and let analysts do the math.

The WARN Act gap is the whole sourcing thesis. Oracle filed for 491 employees in Washington. India alone absorbed roughly 12,000 cuts. The US, Canada, Mexico, and Uruguay took the rest. Workers who pushed back were told that if they were classified as remote and didn't live in California or New York, they didn't qualify for WARN protections at all.
